doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Outside Basie: Monk, Coltrane, Elvin Jones
title: Mingus and the case for happy music
summary: Foster respects Mingus, Monk and Miles but prefers swinging, joyful music, as Basie's was.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: So what did you think of -- I know we’ve got to go, but what did you think about Charlie Mingus?
He was an innovator. He was one in the forefront of whatever. He had his place. I appreciated it. I wouldn’t dare try to usurp on that.
As soon as you say Faubus -­

Yeah, I know, Fables of Faubus. There’s just some people out there that I’m not concerned with getting as far into it as they were, Miles and Mingus and Monk. They had their special place that nobody can invade. As I said before, there’s too much love in my music and too much joy and happiness. I love the idea of playing happy music, happy jazz, happy swinging jazz. That’s what Basie was all about. That music was happy. That’s why people were enjoying it so much. One reason, it swung, it was happy. It made them forget their troubles. That’s what -- I don’t want to remind people of how much hatred and anger we’ve got going. I want to relieve them of it. So I had to back off the avant-garde thing. But with Elvin, I really enjoyed going out there, because he was special. That was a special experience.
